query: W is attractive for plasma-facing divertor components because of its high melting point, thermal resistance, low sputtering yield, and low tritium retention, but its relatively high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature limits use. CuCrZr provides favorable thermal conductivity as a heat sink but has a narrow operating-temperature range and is susceptible to irradiation embrittlement, requiring an intermediate layer that transfers heat efficiently while keeping both materials within suitable temperature ranges. Earlier HEA studies reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, thermal stability in Mo6.6Nb6Ni80Ta1.4Ti6, and favorable combinations of strength and ductility in NbTaTiV, HfNbTaTiZr, and TiVNbTa. Nevertheless, HEA performance can involve tradeoffs among strength, ductility, thermal stability, and phase constitution. TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC dendritic state combines about 800 MPa yield strength with approximately 40% strain, but its reported yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K are only 330 and 423 MPa, respectively, at 30% strain. Under the constraints of efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer, high-temperature mechanical stability, and compatibility with the limited operating ranges of both adjoining materials, what single intervention could improve the TiVNbTa intermediate material? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted change relative to the reported TiVNbTa baseline, temperature and loading boundaries, supporting evidence from the prior HEA results, and a controlled experiment that would falsify both the performance prediction and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of chromium into the TiVNbTa alloy will promote the formation of a multiphase microstructure that enhances high‐temperature strength and ductility, thereby improving its performance as an intermediate layer for efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase BCC dendritic TiVNbTa, with approximately 800 MPa yield strength at room temperature and reduced strengths (yield ~330 MPa, compressive ~423 MPa) at 1273 K.
generation.intervention: Add a low concentration of Cr (e.g., on the order of 5–10 atomic percent) to the TiVNbTa alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Operating temperatures up to 1273 K under tensile and compressive loadings typical of plasma-facing divertor applications, ensuring compatibility with adjacent W and CuCrZr components.
generation.structural_mediator: The Cr addition is expected to induce phase partitioning, causing the emergence of a secondary (or triphasic) microstructure such as a Cr-enriched Laves phase alongside modified BCC phases.
generation.mechanism: The formation of a multiphase microstructure will redistribute internal stresses and obstruct dislocation motion, thereby elevating high-temperature yield strength and compressive strength while maintaining or even improving ductility. This microstructural modification also helps in maintaining suitable thermal conductivities required for effective heat transfer between W and CuCrZr.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline TiVNbTa, the Cr-doped alloy will exhibit significantly enhanced yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K (exceeding 330 and 423 MPa, respectively) with improved ductility, while still being able to effectively transfer heat between W and CuCrZr.
generation.baseline: The current TiVNbTa alloy exhibits a single-phase BCC structure with a yield strength of about 800 MPa at room temperature and reduced strength values at elevated temperatures (yield ~330 MPa and compressive strength ~423 MPa at 1273 K).
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects of Cr addition should be observable within the temperature range up to 1273 K and under loading conditions relevant to a divertor’s operational environment, without compromising the required thermal conductivity between W and CuCrZr.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Cr concentration, the precise nature and distribution of the induced phases, and how these interact under prolonged high-temperature service conditions remain uncertain due to potential kinetic constraints during processing.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of TiVNbTa alloys with varying Cr concentrations (including a control with 0% Cr and samples with 5%, 10%, and 15% Cr). Process all samples under identical conditions and subject them to high-temperature mechanical testing at 1273 K. Conduct microstructural analyses (using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy) to identify phase formation and distribution.
measurements: High-temperature tensile and compressive strength tests
Microstructural characterization (phase identification, morphology, and distribution)
Cyclic thermal stability and fatigue tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Cr addition does not result in the formation of a multiphase microstructure or fails to produce statistically significant improvements in high-temperature yield and compressive strengths (i.e., strength remains at or below the baseline values) and ductility under conditions relevant to divertor applications, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractOvercoming the strength-ductility trade-off in refractory-based high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) is challenging. In this work, simultaneous strength-ductility enhancement of as-cast HfMoTaTiZrCrx refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) was attained through Cr addition. Experimental results reveal that Cr addition induces a unique triphasic microstructure, comprising a Hf/Ti/Zr-enriched BCC1 phase, a Mo/Ta-dominated BCC2 phase, and a Cr/Mo/Ta-dominated C15-type Laves phase. The optimized HfMoTaTiZrCr0.75 alloy achieves σ0.2 of 1982.7 MPa (28% higher than Cr-free HfMoTaTiZr RHEAs) and εf of 12.4% (65% enhancement), representing an outstanding strength among reported as-cast RHEAs with comparable ductility. Microstructural analysis suggests that the uniformly distributed BCC phase redistributes compressive stress and suppresses crack propagation, while the Laves phase enhances strength through Laves phase-induced dislocation obstruction. Simultaneous strength-ductility enhancement of HfMoTaTiZrCrx RHEAs was attained.
